passages.title: Rejected offerings expose the honor people actually give
passages.summary: The LORD tells Israel that he has loved them, and they ask how. He points to his choice of Jacob over Esau. A son honors his father, yet the priests despise God’s name. They ask how they have done so. They offer blind, lame, and sick animals on his altar. God tells them to try giving such gifts to their governor. He would rather the temple doors were shut. His name will be great among the nations.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. No movements or precise worship buildings are reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson asks readers to consider whether their offerings show honor for God. Why does God compare the offerings with gifts presented to a governor?

contextNote.title: Rejected offerings expose the honor people actually give
contextNote.text: The book is built as a series of disputes. God makes a statement, and the people ask how (verses 2, 6, 7). Verse 8 gives a simple test. Would the governor accept a blind or lame animal as a gift? The priests give a human official more honor than God. Leviticus 22:20–22 required animals without defect. Verse 10 says closed doors would be better than such offerings.

passages.title: Public teaching and private fidelity belong within the same dispute
passages.summary: God warns the priests that he will curse their blessings. His covenant with Levi was one of life and peace. A priest’s lips should guard knowledge. These priests have caused many to stumble. The people are also faithless to one another. They weep at the altar because God ignores their offerings. The LORD is witness between each man and the wife of his youth. They have wearied him by asking where the God of justice is.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. No movements or precise worship buildings are reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson uses the complaint about justice to examine attitudes during difficult times. Why can tears at the altar fail to answer betrayal of a spouse?

contextNote.title: Public teaching and private fidelity belong within the same dispute
contextNote.text: Verse 13 shows worshipers weeping because their offerings are not accepted. They ask why. Verse 14 points away from the altar to the home. Each man has been faithless to the wife of his youth. She is called his companion and his wife by covenant. God stood as witness to that promise. The same word, “faithless,” describes the priests’ teaching in verses 10–11.

passages.title: The desired visitor confronts the people who ask for justice
passages.summary: God says he is sending a messenger to prepare his way. The Lord they seek will come suddenly to his temple. He will be like a refiner’s fire and will purify the Levites. He will come near to judge. He will testify against those who cheat workers and oppress widows, orphans, and foreigners. He calls the people to return and stop robbing him of tithes. Some say it is useless to serve God. Those who fear the LORD are written in a book of remembrance.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected geographic references. No movements or precise worship buildings are reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson connects tithing with faith and returning to God. Whose injuries does the judgment name when it answers demands for justice?

contextNote.title: The desired visitor confronts the people who ask for justice
contextNote.text: In 2:17 the people asked where the God of justice was. Verses 1–2 answer that he is coming. They then ask who can stand when he does. Those who called for justice are examined first. Verse 5 lists the charges. Sorcery, adultery, and false oaths stand beside unpaid wages. Wrongs to widows, orphans, and foreigners are named in the same breath.

passages.title: The final warning joins remembered instruction with restored relationships
passages.summary: A day is coming that will burn like a furnace. The proud and the wicked will be like stubble. For those who fear God’s name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing. They will go out leaping like calves from the stall. The people are told to remember the law of Moses. God will send Elijah the prophet before that great day. He will turn the hearts of fathers to their children. He will turn the hearts of children to their fathers.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter names Horeb in remembered instruction. Its uncertain location receives no marker or route.

lds.text: The lesson reads Elijah’s promise through Moroni’s quotation and the later Kirtland Temple account. Why does the final promise concern changed hearts between parents and children?

contextNote.title: The final warning joins remembered instruction with restored relationships
contextNote.text: The book closes with two instructions. Verse 4 looks back: remember the law given through Moses. Verse 5 looks ahead: expect Elijah before the great day. Verse 6 says what Elijah will do. He will turn parents and children toward each other. The healing of families prepares for God’s coming. The other choice is named last, and it is a curse.

words.label: Levites
words.meaning: Members of the tribe of Levi. They cared for the tabernacle and later the temple. The priests came from one Levite family, Aaron’s.

words.label: Covenant
words.meaning: A binding agreement with promises and duties. In the Bible, God makes covenants with people.

words.label: Tithe
words.meaning: A tenth of produce or income given to God.
